newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland, EU move to solve trade disputes.
newsitem.headline: Poland, EU move to solve trade disputes.

text.p: European Commissioner Hans van den Broek announced progress on Friday in resolving trade disputes between Poland and the EU, but said the country could not join the Union soon unless it met all requirements.

He told a news conference after two days of talks in Warsaw that the two sides had signed letters of understanding on vexed issues of Polish protection of its oil and steel sectors, on car part imports and on recognition of EU certificates.

"I think we have made considerable progress with letters signed today in the oil, car and steel sectors and the important question of certification," said van den Broek, who is responsible for EU ties with Eastern Europe.

He gave few details but said both had agreed to refrain from unilateral measures -- a reference to EU charges that Poland had extended protection of its oil and steel sectors without even consulting its EU partners.
Earlier on Friday, he told an international investors' conference that Poland's adjustments to EU standards were well advanced but it still needed major changes to be ready to join.

"No applicant country can afford to relax its reform efforts on the assumption that early membership is guaranteed on political grounds and that gaps in its legal structures or practices can be taken care of after accession through exceptions to rules, known as derogations," van den Broek said.
"New member states will be expected to accept...all the rights and obligations arising from EU treaties and legislation, as a whole, from the date of accession," he added.
Poland, now an EU associate member, hopes to become a full member around the year 2000, possibly with a longer transition period for preparing difficult areas such as agriculture.
Van den Broek told Polish parliamentarians, however, that around the year 2002 was a more likely target, with talks beginning at the end of 1997 or early 1998.
He said adjustments Poland faced ranged from "acceleration of privatisation to the reform of public administration, including civil control of all government departments."

"The Polish banking sector needs root and branch reform, based on sound economic and financial analysis. The government faces a great challenge...in privatising large parts of the banking sector which are under state control," he said.
Van den Broek criticised delays in the privatisation and restructuring of large state-owned companies.

"Many companies are virtually untouched by reform. There has been a tendency to postpone large-scale restructuring in some sectors because of its possible social and political ramifications," he said, branding this "short-term thinking".

The EU has accused Poland of unjustifiably extending tariffs protecting its fuels sector during restructuring until 2000 and not honouring agreements to start removing duties on EU steel from January 1, 1997.

Van den Broek said the EU would offer know-how and consider other help, possibly with the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development and the European Investment Bank, to aid the hard but vital transformation of Poland's steel industry.
"This could prevent maybe further protective measures unilaterally by the Polish government," he said.

The union has also criticised a deal with Daewoo, allowing the South Korean firm to bring 110,000 disassembled cars to Poland duty-free for two years, and long delays in Poland's procedures for accepting EU certificates on imported goods.
Van den Broek said Poland had agreed to speed up alignment with the EU over certification policies.

Foreign Minister Dariusz Rosati told the news conference that the EU had agreed to seek to gradually remove barriers to Polish farm exports, a major priority for Warsaw, and address other Polish complaints, notably over transport policies.
